power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is an escalating global public health concern, contributing significantly to global mortalities and posing a major financial burden, particularly in Low-and Middle-Income Countries (LMICs) like Ghana [Letsa, 2023].
text.formatted: Background: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is an escalating global public health concern, contributing significantly to global mortalities and posing a major financial burden, particularly in Low-and Middle-Income Countries (LMICs) like Ghana <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[Letsa, 2023]</ref>.

text.text: Suboptimal quality of care can lead to severe microvascular complications such as diabetic nephropathy (DN) and opportunistic infections like urinary tract infections (UTIs) [Letsa, 2023].
text.formatted: Suboptimal quality of care can lead to severe microvascular complications such as diabetic nephropathy (DN) and opportunistic infections like urinary tract infections (UTIs) <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[Letsa, 2023]</ref>.

text.text: DN affects 30-40% of diabetics and is a leading cause of end-stage kidney failure, with a reported prevalence of kidney diseases of 12.5% in Ghana [Adoba et al., 2025].
text.formatted: DN affects 30-40% of diabetics and is a leading cause of end-stage kidney failure, with a reported prevalence of kidney diseases of 12.5% in Ghana <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[Adoba et al., 2025]</ref>.

text.text: Given that monitoring quality of care is crucial for prevention, this study aimed to evaluate the quality of DM care indicators, particularly focusing on urinary biomarkers, at the Ghana Ports and Harbours Authority (GPHA) hospital.
Methodology: A cross-sectional design employing a retrospective medical audit was utilized, assessing patient records at the GPHA hospital Diabetes Clinic.

The study population comprised 125 participants whose urinalysis data, demographics, and comorbidity categorization (Diabetes only, Diabetes and Hypertension, Diabetes and Cyesis, etc.) were collected.
Urine parameters, including albuminuria, glucose, and Renal Tubular Epithelial Cells (RTEC), were retrieved from Sysmex's urinalysis analyzers (Sysmex UC 400, UF 350).
Results: The study cohort consisted predominantly of females (58.4%, n=73) with a mean age of 54.92 years .
The primary diabetic categorization was "diabetes only" (76.8%, n=96).
Evaluation of albuminuria showed that mild albuminuria was recorded for only 10.4% (n=13) of participants, and overt albuminuria was absent (0.0%).
This mild albuminuria prevalence is notably below the 25-30% global prevalence reported for type 2 diabetics.

Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a rapidly escalating global health crisis, responsible for a significant increase in mortalities since the early 2000s and now ranking among the top ten causes of death worldwide.

In 2021, the International Diabetes Federation (IDF) reported 537 million adults aged 20 to 79 living with diabetes, a figure projected to rise to 783 million by 2045, with 94% of this increase anticipated in low-and middle-income countries (LMICs) [Letsa, 2023].

text.text: Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) is expected to experience the fastest rise in diabetes prevalence, facing a "double burden of disease" where diabetes exacerbates infection risks and strains limited healthcare resources [Letsa, 2023].

text.text: The global expenditure on diabetes reached 966 billion dollars in 2021, with Africa alone accounting for approximately 13 billion dollars [Letsa, 2023].
text.formatted: The global expenditure on diabetes reached 966 billion dollars in 2021, with Africa alone accounting for approximately 13 billion dollars <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[Letsa, 2023]</ref>.

text.text: Diabetes is associated with severe macrovascular and microvascular complications [Letsa, 2023].

text.text: Diabetic nephropathy (DN), a major microvascular complication, affects 30-40% of diabetics and is a leading cause of end-stage kidney failure, contributing significantly to healthcare costs and cardiovascular morbidity [Sorvor et al., 2022 , Adoba et al., 2025].

text.text: This study aims to address these critical research gaps by evaluating the quality of diabetes care at the Ghana Ports and Harbours Authority (GPHA) hospital using NDQIA-approved quality indicators [Letsa, 2023].
text.formatted: This study aims to address these critical research gaps by evaluating the quality of diabetes care at the Ghana Ports and Harbours Authority (GPHA) hospital using NDQIA-approved quality indicators <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[Letsa, 2023]</ref>.

text.text: The general objective of this study was to through a medical audit, utilizing the quality indicators approved by the National Diabetes Quality Improvement Alliance (NDQIA) of the United States [Letsa, 2023].
text.formatted: The general objective of this study was to through a medical audit, utilizing the quality indicators approved by the National Diabetes Quality Improvement Alliance (NDQIA) of the United States <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[Letsa, 2023]</ref>.

text.text: This study employed a cross-sectional design, primarily involving a retrospective medical audit of patient records at the Diabetes Clinic of the GPHA hospital in Ghana.
The GPHA Diabetes Clinic is a weekly clinic at the GPHA hospital, Takoradi that sees approximately 30 to 40 clients weekly and is headed by a Senior medical doctor.

The study population comprised clients whose urinalysis data were collected between 25 July 2022 and 30 November 2022, during which period Sysmex urinalysis analyzers UC 350 and UF 400 were procured and used.

Participants were included if their diagnosis, retrieved from the hospital management system using their unique laboratory numbers, fell into one of the following categories: cyesis and diabetes only, diabetes and hypertension only, diabetes only, or cyesis diabetes hypertension only.
This approach allowed for the linkage of specific laboratory findings to patient diagnoses.
Data collection was conducted in two main parts: 1.

Urinalysis and Structural/Input Measures: Urinalysis Data: Demographic data (age and gender) as well as urinalysis data comprising urobilinogen, blood, bilirubin, ketones, protein, pH, nitrite, leukocyte, creatinine, albumin, protein creatinine ratio, albumin creatinine ratio, specific gravity, color, appearance, RTEC, conductivity and osmolality were retrieved from the Sysmex UC 350 urine analyser.

Clinical Process and Outcome Indicators: With approval from hospital authority and patient's anonymised, a retrospective medical audit of the diagnosis of the selected patient records was retrieved by both a laboratory personnel and a nursing staff.
Retrieved data was reviewed by a team of laboratory personnel to confirm data correctness and accuracy.
Prior to data collection, research assistants received training on the study's aims, data abstraction procedures, and ethical guidelines.
The data abstraction tool was pre-tested on 50 subjects at the hospital to identify and rectify any gaps in the tool and procedure.
Collected data were first entered into Microsoft Excel 2021 and subsequently exported to Stata MP 17.0 for analysis.
Descriptive statistics, such as means, standard deviations, frequencies, and proportions, were used to summarise both continuous and categorical variables.
A univariate analysis of background characteristics was conducted and reported in numbers and percentages.

text.text: The age of study subjects ranged from 28 to 76 years with a mean of 54.92.
Majority (55.2%) of the participants belonged to the 45-64 years category, 23.20% were above 64 years and the remaining 21.6% were in the 25-44 years group (Table 2).

This information suggests that persons who are 40 years and above are at higher risk to diabetes in a similar population.
Again, the study showed that 21.6% subjects below 45 years had diabetes.
This is comparable to current global diabetes trends of 20-25% (WHO, 2024).

About 82.4% (103) of the study subjects did not record glucose in their urine, 2.4% (3) had trace, and the remaining 15.2% (19) presented varying levels of glucosuria (Table 4).

text.text: The primary findings of this study highlight the prevalence of key urine biomarkersalbuminuria, proteinuria, glucosuria, and Renal Tubular Epithelial Cells (RTEC)-among diabetic patients at the GPHA hospital and analyze their association with diabetic comorbidities.
The demographic profile of the participants, showing a mean age of 54.92 years and a female majority (58.4%), is consistent with general observations in Ghana and the sub-region [Letsa, 2023].
text.formatted: The demographic profile of the participants, showing a mean age of 54.92 years and a female majority (58.4%), is consistent with general observations in Ghana and the sub-region <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[Letsa, 2023]</ref>.

text.text: For instance, a previous study in Kumasi reported a comparable mean age of 54.1 years [Eghan and Adjei-Poku, 2007].
text.formatted: For instance, a previous study in Kumasi reported a comparable mean age of 54.1 years <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[Eghan and Adjei-Poku, 2007]</ref>.

text.text: The high female attendance (58.4%) aligns with documented trends where females are generally more proactive in seeking and reporting for regular health reviews compared to their male counterparts [Letsa, 2023].
text.formatted: The high female attendance (58.4%) aligns with documented trends where females are generally more proactive in seeking and reporting for regular health reviews compared to their male counterparts <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[Letsa, 2023]</ref>.

text.text: The evaluation of albuminuria revealed a low prevalence of early diabetic nephropathy markers in the studied population.
Specifically, mild albuminuria (MA) was recorded in only 10.4% of participants, and overt albuminuria was completely absent (0.0%).
This figure is significantly lower than the generally accepted global prevalence of microalbuminuria (25-30%) among type 2 diabetics.

Furthermore, this finding contrasts markedly with other reports from Ghana, where a study in Kumasi found a microalbuminuria prevalence of 43.1% in diabetic patients, while another multicentre study reported a prevalence of significant CKD (stages 3-5) at 44.3% among Ghanaian patients with hypertension and diabetes [Eghan and Adjei-Poku, 2007, Sorvor et al., 2022].
text.formatted: Furthermore, this finding contrasts markedly with other reports from Ghana, where a study in Kumasi found a microalbuminuria prevalence of 43.1% in diabetic patients, while another multicentre study reported a prevalence of significant CKD (stages 3-5) at 44.3% among Ghanaian patients with hypertension and diabetes <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[Eghan and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Adjei-Poku, 2007, Sorvor et al., 2022]</ref>.

text.text: The low prevalence observed in this study may be attributed to inherent limitations, including the small sample size and the inability to differentiate diabetes types (Type 1 vs.
Type 2) or ascertain medication details, which limits comparison to external studies.
Nonetheless, microalbuminuria is recognized as a crucial, early marker for renal involvement in diabetes and its monitoring is strongly recommended [Eghan and Adjei-Poku, 2007].
text.formatted: Nonetheless, microalbuminuria is recognized as a crucial, early marker for renal involvement in diabetes and its monitoring is strongly recommended <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[Eghan and Adjei-Poku, 2007]</ref>.

text.text: The study noted that overall kidney dysfunction (defined by GFR abnormalities) remains a significant concern in Ghana, with a cross-sectional study in the Obuasi East Municipality reporting a total prevalence of 32.35%, comprising 23.5% hyperfiltration and 8.82% low GFR (<90 mL/min/1.73m²) [Adoba et al., 2025].
text.formatted: The study noted that overall kidney dysfunction (defined by GFR abnormalities) remains a significant concern in Ghana, with a cross-sectional study in the Obuasi East Municipality reporting a total prevalence of 32.35%, comprising 23.5% hyperfiltration and 8.82% low GFR (<90 mL/min/1.73m²) <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[Adoba et al., 2025]</ref>.

text.text: Regionally, a systematic review noted that the pooled prevalence of nephropathy in West Africa (including Ghana) was 11%, the lowest among African regions studied [Sorvor et al., 2022].
text.formatted: Regionally, a systematic review noted that the pooled prevalence of nephropathy in West Africa (including Ghana) was 11%, the lowest among African regions studied <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[Sorvor et al., 2022]</ref>.

text.text: The detection of pathological Renal Tubular Epithelial Cells (RTEC) in a few individuals (3 out of 26 tested), particularly those with concurrent diabetes and hypertension, suggests that structural kidney damage indicators appear primarily in patients with established comorbidities.
A notable outcome was the significant correlation found between the various diabetic population categories and urine glucose (Pr=0.001).
While a majority of subjects (82.4%) recorded no urine glucose, 15.2% presented varying levels of glucosuria .

This association indicates that the severity or complexity of the diabetic condition, reflected by comorbidity (e.g., hypertension, cyesis), influences glycemic control as measured by urinary glucose excretion.

The presence of glucose in the urine promotes bacterial growth, significantly increasing the diabetic patient's susceptibility to Urinary Tract Infections (UTIs) due to the compromised immune system associated with DM [ Kangume, 2024].

text.text: The study was limited by its cross-sectional design, the small sample size, and the challenge in documenting the specific type of diabetes, medication, and the level of complication, which restricts a comprehensive comparison against NDQIA quality outcome targets.
Nevertheless, the focus on specific urinary biomarkers provides unique baseline data for the GPHA clinic .
Future efforts should emphasize addressing the research gap regarding the quality of diabetes care specifically evaluated through comprehensive care indicators [ Letsa, 2023].
text.formatted: Future efforts should emphasize addressing the research gap regarding the quality of diabetes care specifically evaluated through comprehensive care indicators <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[ Letsa, 2023]</ref>.

text.text: The continued evaluation of diagnostic efficiency for newer markers like serum free light chains (which showed promise but required further elucidation in other Ghanaian studies) remains important for early detection of DN [Sorvor et al., 2022].

text.text: Diabetes mellitus continues to impose a significant health burden globally, requiring optimal quality of care to mitigate its associated complications and mortality [Letsa, 2023].
text.formatted: Diabetes mellitus continues to impose a significant health burden globally, requiring optimal quality of care to mitigate its associated complications and mortality <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[Letsa, 2023]</ref>.

text.text: This study at the GPHA hospital found that the prevalence of mild albuminuria (10.4%) was remarkably low compared to established international and many national benchmarks.
Conversely, a significant correlation was established between the complexity of the diabetic population (comorbidities) and urine glucose levels (Pr=0.001).
Given that kidney involvement in diabetes is a major cause of subsequent morbidity and mortality, continued adherence to strict monitoring guidelines is imperative [Eghan and Adjei-Poku, 2007].
